34.1 i ntroduction
We have examined a number of ways of analyzing the data generated by an experiment, but
have not dealt with creating the experiment. How does a researcher construct an experi-
ment? What factors are important in its design? These are the fundamental questions in the
area of experimental design.
Experimental design is the area of investigation dealing with the structure and
planning of experiments.
34.2 c lassification of d esigns
The purpose of an experiment is to discover the effect of certain independent variables on a
dependent variable. The outcome of the experiment will be measured in terms of variation
in the value of the dependent variable.
Often, an effort will be made to control the possible effects of (independent) variables not
intended to be part of the experiment whose presence might influence the value of the
dependent variable and thereby muddy the results. A completely randomized block design
maintains such control by appropriate construction of the experiment, while the analysis of
covariance model is a statistical technique to control the effects of extraneous variables or
concomitant examples.
Another goal in experimental design is the maintenance of a balance between replicability
of the research results and the ability to generalize them. Certainly it is desirable that the
researcher be able to extend the results of his study to individuals, cases, or situations that
were not part of the experiment, but it should also be possible for others to replicate his
results.
Before we define types of experimental designs that might meet these goals, we first distin-
guish between two approaches to applied research:
Experimental research occurs when the experimenter manipulates certain
independent variables, while controlling the effects of others.
Ex post facto research occurs when the experimenter observes values of the
independent variables whose effects on the dependent variable are being studied,
while controlling the effects of others.
Note that in experimental research, the experimenter determines values of the independent
variables being examined, while in ex post facto research, he observes values of the
independent variables but does not influence them.
c H apter 34 n e xper IM ental Des IG ns n n n 437
The statistical analyses applied to the data are not determined by the type of research
employed. They will be the same in either case, and the following algorithm describes the
analytical process:

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 34.1 Introduction
chunks.content:
Step 1: Observe the system to be studied.
Step 2: If the problem is defined, continue; ELSE go to Step 1.
Step 3: If variables can be identified, continue; ELSE go to Step 1.
Step 4: If hypotheses can be formulated, continue; ELSE go to Step 2.
Step 5: Establish the research design.
Step 6: Determine the sampling procedures.
Step 7: Collect the data.
Step 8: Perform the statistical analysis.
Step 9: Interpret the results.
Step 10: If results correspond to the problem, continue; ELSE go to Step 5.
Step 11: Report the results.
When we identify ways to control the variation of extraneous independent variables, we have
completely described the components of the system under study: the dependent variable,
the independent variables whose effects on the dependent variable concern us, and other
independent variables whose influence on the dependent variable we wish to control. There
are four major methods for controlling the impact of these control variables:
n Holding such variables constant
n Randomizing their effects
n Matching experimental units with respect to values of the control variables
n Controlling their impact statistically
We have used the technique of holding all the independent variables constant except the one
being studied when we observed the drop in R
2
from the full to a reduced model in multiple
linear regression. Randomization is possibly the “best” method of control; experimental units
are assigned randomly to the various experimental treatments (values of the independent
variable being studied) with respect to values of the control variables. There are several ways
to match experimental units to control the impact of an independent variable. In one, the
elements of the experimental group are stratified by values of the control variable, and these
strata are then distributed among the treatments. In another, the sample is divided into equal
parts corresponding to the number of values of the control variable, and the experiment is
repeated several times. Finally, control can be achieved statistically whenever the control
variable is correlated with the dependent variable, since the control variable then accounts
438 n n n r esearch Metho D s for Infor M at I on s yste M s n c Hapter 34
for part of the variation of the dependent variable. The researcher need only eliminate that
portion of the variation from the analysis.
34.3 e xperimental d esign d efinitions
Classical experimental design:
n Two groups are formed either by random assignment or by matching.
n Two groups are identical before the experiment begins.
n During the experiment, one group (the treatment group) receives the experimental
treatment and the other (the control group) does not.
n After the experiment, differences in the values of the dependent variable from the
control to the treatment group can thus be attributed to the experimental treatment.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 34.1 Introduction
chunks.content:
Often, practical limitations—cost, time, etc.—prevent this design from being fully real-
ized. In some cases, for example, a similar but nonequivalent control group is used. Or the
researcher will construct a comparison group by dividing an intact group into treatment and
comparison components, according to the value of some measure taken before administra-
tion of the experimental treatment. Designs with nonequivalent control groups are called
quasi-experimental designs.
The simplest experimental design is called the simple randomized design:
Simple randomized design:
n Only one independent variable and the dependent variable are included in the
analysis.
n Control is achieved by randomization, and possibly by holding other variables
constant.
One-way analysis of variance is an example of such a design when the dependent variable is
interval level. When the dependent variable is nominal, we have used the chi-square test.
The inclusion of more independent variables in the analysis leads to factorial designs in which
the researcher conducts several experiments simultaneously with the same experimental
units, and the possible effects of interactions between independent variables can be studied.
We make the following definition.
Factorial designs:
n Two or more independent variables, called factors, are studied simultaneously.
n No provisions are made for controlling the effects of other independent variables
on the dependent variable other than randomization and possibly holding control
variables constant.

Whether the hypotheses of equal row means or interaction are to be tested will be a function

Such a design has three distinct advantages over a simple randomized design:
n The stratification gives some control over the blocking variable.
n Because of the stratification, the analysis is more sensitive to possible relations
between the dependent variable and the factor.
n Data for the independent variable can be studied separately.
Both analysis of variance and multiple regression can be used with the randomized block
design.
If the effects of all treatments are temporary, the researcher may use a repeated measure
design.
Repeated measure design:
The experimental treatments are administered in order to each experimental unit.
The statistical techniques applied to data generated by such a design are the same as those
used with a randomized block design.

Analysis of covariance extends the classical experimental designs described above by com-
bining techniques of prediction with the analysis of variance. Prediction of the dependent
variable from the control variables allows the adjustment of the values of the dependent vari-
able. These adjusted values are then analyzed using the usual experimental designs.
34.4 a voiding p itfalls
In any research endeavor, it is wise to follow these guidelines:
n Select a meaningful dependent variable.
n When using a pre-test, do not use both selection and control experimental units with
the same measurements for the dependent variable.
n If only one set of measurements of the dependent variable is used, when the
selection is made it will alter the results of the control mechanism by what is called
the regression effect.
n Use the same instrument for pre- and post-testing.
n Make sure the treatment and control groups are comparable.
n When the treatment and control groups are nonequivalent, use the appropriate
statistical adjustments. In particular, avoid the use of raw gain scores, which are the
differences between pre- and post-test scores, unless the standard deviations of the

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: ON DVD
chunks.content:
pre- and post-test scores are equal.
n Do not construct a matched control group after the treatment group has been
selected. If this is done, regression will act differently on the two groups and will
inflate apparent differences. Be careful in the collection of data.
n Avoid missing data. The analysis should be based on experimental units present in
both control and experimental groups.
n Do not generalize beyond the information extracted from the experiment and the
results of the statistical analysis.
34.5 e xperimental g oals
Upon completion of his research, the researcher should be able to answer the following
questions:
n Is there a significant difference in the value of the dependent variable that can be
attributed to one or more of the factors?
n Is this difference statistically significant?
442 n n n r esearch Metho D s for Infor M at I on s yste M s n c Hapter 34
n Is the effect of factors on the dependent variable significant in terms of the problem?
n Can the treatments of the experiment be applied in another setting with a reasonable
expectation of similar results?
n How likely is it that the observed effects are the results of the treatments?
n Are the results believable and interpretable?
